notes:
Werner's Theory & Terminology

  • Metals show two types of valency: primary (ionisable, satisfied by anions, = oxidation state) and secondary (non-ionisable, fixed, = coordination number, satisfied by ligands in a fixed geometry).
  • Coordination entity: central atom/ion + ligands, e.g. [Co(NH$_3$)$_6$]$^{3+}$. Counter ion balances charge outside the bracket.
  • Ligand types: unidentate (Cl$^-$, NH$_3$), bidentate (en = ethylenediamine, ox$^{2-}$ = oxalate), polydentate (EDTA$^{4-}$, hexadentate). Ambidentate ligands (e.g. -NO$_2$/-ONO, -SCN/-NCS) bind through either of two donor atoms.
  • Coordination number = number of ligand donor atoms bonded to the central metal. Common CN: 4 (tetrahedral/square planar), 6 (octahedral).
  • Oxidation state of central metal = charge it would carry if all ligands are removed with their bonding electron pairs.

Nomenclature (IUPAC)

  • Order: cation named first regardless of charge; ligands named in alphabetical order before the metal (prefixes di, tri... or bis, tris... for complex-named ligands are not counted for alphabetising).
  • Anionic ligands end in -o (chlorido, cyanido, oxalato); neutral ligands keep their name (aqua, ammine, carbonyl for CO, nitrosyl for NO); if the complex ion is anionic, metal name ends in -ate (ferrate, cuprate) with the Latin name where applicable.
  • Oxidation state of metal shown in Roman numeral in brackets immediately after its name.

Isomerism

TypeDescription
IonisationDifferent ions produced in solution, e.g. [Co(NH$_3$)$_5$Br]SO$_4$ vs [Co(NH$_3$)$_5$SO$_4$]Br
Hydrate/SolvateWater inside vs outside coordination sphere, e.g. [Cr(H$_2$O)$_6$]Cl$_3$ vs [Cr(H$_2$O)$_5$Cl]Cl$_2$.H$_2$O
LinkageAmbidentate ligand bonds through different atoms, e.g. -NO$_2$ vs -ONO
CoordinationDistribution of ligands between cation and anion complexes differs
Geometricalcis-trans in square planar/octahedral (e.g. [Pt(NH$_3$)$_2$Cl$_2$])
OpticalNon-superimposable mirror images, common in octahedral complexes with bidentate ligands, e.g. [Co(en)$_3$]$^{3+}$

Bonding Theories

  • VBT: hybridisation decides geometry — sp$^3$ (tetrahedral), dsp$^2$ (square planar), sp$^3d^2$/$d^2sp^3$ (octahedral, outer/inner orbital resp.).
  • Crystal Field Theory (CFT): ligands split degenerate d orbitals. Octahedral field: $t_{2g}$ (lower, 3 orbitals) and $e_g$ (higher, 2 orbitals), splitting energy $\Delta_o$. Strong field ligands (CN$^-$, CO) cause large $\Delta_o$ $\to$ pairing $\to$ low spin; weak field ligands (F$^-$, H$_2$O, halides) give small $\Delta_o$ $\to$ high spin (for $d^4$-$d^7$).
  • Spectrochemical series (increasing field strength): I$^- <$ Br$^- <$ Cl$^- <$ F$^- <$ H$_2$O $<$ NH$_3$ $<$ en $<$ CN$^- <$ CO.
  • CFSE and pairing energy together decide high spin vs low spin for $d^4$–$d^7$ octahedral complexes.

Colour, Magnetism & Applications

  • Colour arises from d-d transitions (needs partially filled d orbitals and a ligand field to split them). $[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}$ is diamagnetic square planar, but $[NiCl_4]^{2-}$ is paramagnetic tetrahedral (weak field Cl$^-$).
  • Applications: cisplatin (anticancer), EDTA (treatment of lead poisoning, water hardness estimation), silver/gold extraction (as cyanide complexes), chlorophyll (Mg complex), haemoglobin (Fe complex), electroplating, catalysts (Wilkinson's catalyst).

Exam tip

KCET typically sets 3-4 questions here: expect one on CFT/spectrochemical series (high spin vs low spin), one on IUPAC naming, one on isomerism type identification, and one on coordination number/oxidation state calculation.

questions.q: In the complex $[Co(NH_3)_5Cl]Cl_2$, the coordination number and oxidation state of cobalt are respectively
questions.explanation: Co is bonded to 5 NH$_3$ and 1 Cl inside the bracket, giving coordination number 6. The two Cl outside the bracket are counter ions ($-1$ each), so Co is $+3$ to balance overall neutrality.
questions.trick: Only ligands inside the bracket count for CN; outside ions are counter ions balancing charge.

questions.q: The IUPAC name of $[Co(NH_3)_6]Cl_3$ is
questions.explanation: The cation is named first (ligands alphabetically then metal with oxidation state in Roman numerals), followed by the anion name: hexaamminecobalt(III) chloride.
questions.trick: Name order: cation first, ligands alphabetical, then metal(oxidation state), anion last.

questions.q: Which of the following ligands is an example of an ambidentate ligand?
questions.explanation: An ambidentate ligand can coordinate through either of two different donor atoms; thiocyanate can bind through S (-SCN) or N (-NCS), unlike en (bidentate, N,N-donor) or oxalate (bidentate, O,O-donor).
questions.trick: Ambidentate = two possible donor atoms; SCN$^-$ binds via S or N.

questions.q: $[Co(NH_3)_5Br]SO_4$ and $[Co(NH_3)_5SO_4]Br$ are examples of
questions.explanation: These two compounds give different ions in solution (Br$^-$ vs SO$_4^{2-}$ as the free counter ion) despite having the same molecular formula, characteristic of ionisation isomerism.
questions.trick: Different free ion released in water $\to$ ionisation isomerism.

questions.q: According to crystal field theory, in an octahedral complex the d orbitals split into
options: all five orbitals of equal energy
questions.explanation: In an octahedral field, ligands approach along the axes, raising the energy of $d_{z^2}, d_{x^2-y^2}$ ($e_g$) more than $d_{xy}, d_{yz}, d_{zx}$ ($t_{2g}$), which lie between the axes; so $t_{2g}$ is lower and $e_g$ is higher, separated by $\Delta_o$.
questions.trick: Octahedral: ligands hit $e_g$ head-on (higher), miss $t_{2g}$ (lower).

questions.q: Which of these ligands is a strong field ligand, favouring a low-spin complex?
questions.explanation: In the spectrochemical series, CN$^-$ lies near the strong-field end, causing large $\Delta_o$, so electrons preferentially pair up in $t_{2g}$ rather than occupy $e_g$, giving a low-spin complex.
questions.trick: Spectrochemical series: CN$^-$/CO far right $\to$ large $\Delta_o$ $\to$ low spin.

questions.q: $[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}$ is diamagnetic and square planar, while $[NiCl_4]^{2-}$ is paramagnetic and tetrahedral. This is because
options: the two complexes have different coordination numbers
Ni has different oxidation states in the two complexes
Cl$^-$ is a stronger field ligand than CN$^-$
CN$^-$ is a strong field ligand causing pairing of electrons (dsp$^2$), while Cl$^-$ is weak field, leaving electrons unpaired (sp$^3$)
questions.explanation: In both complexes Ni is +2 (d$^8$). Strong field CN$^-$ causes pairing of the two unpaired electrons giving dsp$^2$ hybridisation (square planar, diamagnetic); weak field Cl$^-$ does not cause pairing, giving sp$^3$ hybridisation (tetrahedral, paramagnetic with 2 unpaired electrons).
questions.trick: Strong field CN$^-$ pairs $d^8$ (dsp$^2$, square planar); weak Cl$^-$ doesn't (sp$^3$, tetrahedral).

questions.q: The number of geometrical isomers possible for the square planar complex $[Pt(NH_3)_2Cl_2]$ is
questions.explanation: A square planar MA$_2$B$_2$ complex can have the two identical ligands adjacent (cis) or opposite (trans) to each other, giving exactly 2 geometrical isomers.
questions.trick: Square planar MA$_2$B$_2$ always gives exactly cis + trans = 2 isomers.

questions.q: Which octahedral complex is expected to show optical isomerism?
questions.explanation: $[Co(en)_3]^{3+}$, with three symmetric bidentate ligands wrapped around the octahedral centre, is chiral and exists as non-superimposable mirror-image (optical) isomers, unlike the fully symmetric $[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}$.
questions.trick: Chiral needs no mirror plane: three bidentate ligands like $[Co(en)_3]^{3+}$ twist chirally.

questions.q: EDTA is used medicinally in the treatment of poisoning by which metal?
questions.explanation: EDTA (a hexadentate ligand) forms a stable, water-soluble chelate with Pb$^{2+}$, which is then excreted, making it useful in treating lead poisoning.
questions.trick: EDTA + lead poisoning is a fixed textbook pair — memorise it.

questions.q: Cisplatin, $[Pt(NH_3)_2Cl_2]$ (cis isomer), is used clinically as
questions.explanation: cis-[Pt(NH$_3$)$_2$Cl$_2$] (cisplatin) binds to DNA in cancer cells and inhibits replication, and is widely used as an anticancer chemotherapy drug; the trans isomer is biologically inactive.
questions.trick: cis-Platin fights cancer; trans isomer is biologically inactive.

questions.q: The oxidation state of iron in $[Fe(CN)_6]^{4-}$ is
questions.explanation: CN$^-$ ligands each carry a $-1$ charge; 6 CN$^-$ give $-6$. For overall charge $-4$: $x + (-6) = -4 \Rightarrow x = +2$.
questions.trick: Balance charge: metal + (ligand charges) = overall ionic charge.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes a chelate ligand?
options: A ligand that can only bind through carbon
A polydentate ligand that binds through two or more donor atoms to the same metal, forming a ring
A unidentate ligand that binds weakly
A neutral ligand with no donor atoms
questions.explanation: A chelating ligand has two or more donor atoms that simultaneously bond to the same central metal ion, forming a ring (chelate) structure, which generally gives added stability (chelate effect), e.g. en, EDTA, oxalate.
questions.trick: Chelate = polydentate ligand forming a ring with one metal centre.

questions.q: In Werner's theory, the secondary valency of a metal ion corresponds to its
questions.explanation: Werner defined secondary valency as the fixed number of ligand donor atoms directly bonded to the metal in a definite spatial arrangement — this is what we now call the coordination number.
questions.trick: Werner: secondary valency = fixed ligand count = coordination number.

questions.q: A complex of the type $[M(en)_2Cl_2]^+$ (octahedral, en = bidentate) can show
options: cis and trans geometrical isomers, with the cis form also being optically active
questions.explanation: $[M(en)_2Cl_2]^+$ shows geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism; the cis form lacks a plane of symmetry and is chiral (optically active), while the trans form has a plane of symmetry and is optically inactive.
questions.trick: cis-$[M(en)_2X_2]$ lacks a mirror plane $\to$ chiral; trans has one $\to$ inactive.

questions.q: According to valence bond theory, an octahedral complex using $d^2sp^3$ (inner orbital) hybridisation is generally
options: a high-spin, weak-field complex with more unpaired electrons
a low-spin, strong-field complex, more stable and often diamagnetic/less paramagnetic
questions.explanation: Inner orbital ($d^2sp^3$) complexes use the inner $(n-1)d$ orbitals, which happens when strong field ligands force electron pairing, leading to low-spin, generally more stable complexes (as opposed to outer orbital $sp^3d^2$, high-spin complexes with weak field ligands).
questions.trick: Inner orbital $d^2sp^3$ = strong field forced pairing = low spin, stable.

questions.q: The complex $[Cr(H_2O)_6]Cl_3$ and $[Cr(H_2O)_5Cl]Cl_2\cdot H_2O$ are related by
questions.explanation: These isomers differ in whether a water molecule is inside the coordination sphere or present as water of crystallisation outside it — this is hydrate (solvate) isomerism.
questions.trick: Water inside vs outside the bracket $\to$ hydrate (solvate) isomerism.

questions.q: Which statement about the colour of transition metal complexes is correct?
options: Colour depends only on the counter ion, never the central metal
Colour arises from d-d electronic transitions made possible by ligand field splitting of d orbitals
Colour arises because ligands absorb all visible light equally
questions.explanation: When ligands split the d orbitals (CFT), electrons can be promoted from a lower ($t_{2g}$) to a higher ($e_g$) d orbital by absorbing visible light of energy $\Delta_o$; the transmitted complementary colour is what we observe.
questions.trick: Colour needs partly filled d orbitals split by ligand field (d-d transition).

questions.q: The name of the ligand Cl$^-$ and the anionic complex ending used when the whole complex ion is negatively charged are respectively
questions.explanation: In current IUPAC nomenclature, Cl$^-$ as a ligand is named 'chlorido', and when the overall complex ion is an anion, the metal name takes the suffix '-ate' (e.g. ferrate, cobaltate).
questions.trick: Cl$^-$ ligand = 'chlorido'; anionic whole complex $\to$ metal ends in '-ate'.

questions.q: Which of the following is used in the extraction of silver and gold via complex formation?
questions.explanation: Silver and gold ores are leached with dilute NaCN solution in the presence of air; the metals form soluble cyanide complexes $[Ag(CN)_2]^-$/$[Au(CN)_2]^-$, from which the pure metal is later displaced by a more reactive metal like zinc.
questions.trick: Ag/Au leaching: dilute NaCN forms soluble $[M(CN)_2]^-$ complexes.

questions.q: The coordination number and oxidation number of platinum in $[Pt(en)_2Cl_2]$ are
questions.explanation: Each en is bidentate (2 donor atoms each, so 2 en = 4) plus 2 Cl = coordination number 6. en is neutral, Cl$^-$ contributes $-2$, so for the neutral complex Pt is $+2$ (Pt $+ 0 + (-2) = 0$).
questions.trick: Bidentate en gives 2 donor atoms each; count donors, then balance charge for oxidation state.

questions.q: Which of the following complexes is expected to be colourless?
questions.explanation: Zn$^{2+}$ is $d^{10}$ (fully filled d subshell), so no d-d transition is possible and the complex is colourless; Ti$^{3+}$ ($d^1$), Cu$^{2+}$ ($d^9$) and Ni$^{2+}$ ($d^8$) all have partially filled d orbitals and are coloured.
questions.trick: $d^{10}$ metals (Zn$^{2+}$) have no d-d transition $\to$ colourless.

questions.q: The CFSE (crystal field stabilisation energy) for a high-spin $d^5$ octahedral complex is
options: zero (all orbitals singly occupied, no net stabilisation)
questions.explanation: High-spin $d^5$ places one electron in each of the five d orbitals ($t_{2g}^3 e_g^2$); since $3(-0.4\Delta_o) + 2(+0.6\Delta_o) = 0$, the net CFSE is zero.
questions.trick: High-spin $d^5$: $3(-0.4)+2(0.6)=0$, so CFSE is always zero.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a homoleptic complex?
questions.explanation: A homoleptic complex has only one type of ligand bonded to the metal; $[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}$ has six identical NH$_3$ ligands, while the others are heteroleptic (mixed ligands).
questions.trick: Homoleptic = one ligand type only; mixed ligands = heteroleptic.

questions.q: Linkage isomerism is possible in $[Co(NH_3)_5(NO_2)]Cl_2$ because the nitrito ligand can bind through
options: carbon in one form and nitrogen in the other
either its nitrogen atom (nitro, -NO$_2$) or an oxygen atom (nitrito, -ONO)
questions.explanation: NO$_2^-$ is an ambidentate ligand: it can coordinate via N (nitro form) or via O (nitrito form), giving rise to linkage isomers of the same overall formula.
questions.trick: NO$_2^-$ ambidentate: nitro binds via N, nitrito binds via O.

questions.q: According to IUPAC rules, when naming a complex ion with more than one kind of ligand, the ligands are cited in the name in
options: alphabetical order, irrespective of their number or charge
questions.explanation: IUPAC nomenclature lists ligand names alphabetically (ignoring multiplying prefixes like di-, tri-, bis-), before naming the central metal atom.
questions.trick: Ligands cited alphabetically in the name; ignore di-/tri-/bis- prefixes for ordering.

questions.q: The complex $[Co(NH_3)_5H_2O]Cl_3$ reacts with excess AgNO$_3$ solution. The number of moles of AgCl precipitated per mole of complex is
questions.explanation: All three Cl$^-$ ions lie outside the coordination sphere as counter ions (H$_2$O occupies the sixth coordination site), so all three are freely ionisable and precipitate as 3 mol AgCl.
questions.trick: Only ions outside the coordination sphere are free to precipitate with AgNO$_3$.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the spectrochemical series is INCORRECT?
options: H$_2$O is a weaker field ligand than NH$_3$
I$^-$ is a weaker field ligand than Cl$^-$
CO is a stronger field ligand than NH$_3$
F$^-$ is a stronger field ligand than CN$^-$
questions.explanation: In the spectrochemical series CN$^-$ is a much stronger field ligand than F$^-$; the correct increasing order is I$^- <$ Br$^- <$ Cl$^- <$ F$^- <$ H$_2$O $<$ NH$_3 <$ en $<$ CN$^- <$ CO.
questions.trick: Series order: I$^-<$Br$^-<$Cl$^-<$F$^-<$H$_2$O$<$NH$_3<$en$<$CN$^-<$CO — CN$^-$ beats F$^-$.

questions.q: Wilkinson's catalyst, $[RhCl(PPh_3)_3]$, is industrially important because it catalyses
options: hydrogenation of alkenes under mild conditions
questions.explanation: Wilkinson's catalyst is a homogeneous rhodium complex widely used to catalyse the hydrogenation of alkenes at low temperature and pressure.
questions.trick: Wilkinson's catalyst $[RhCl(PPh_3)_3]$ = mild alkene hydrogenation, memorise the pairing.

questions.q: For a complex $[MA_4B_2]$ (octahedral, A and B unidentate), how many geometrical isomers are possible?
questions.explanation: An octahedral MA$_4$B$_2$ complex shows cis (B ligands adjacent, 90°) and trans (B ligands opposite, 180°) arrangements — exactly 2 geometrical isomers.
questions.trick: Octahedral MA$_4$B$_2$: B pair adjacent (cis, 90°) or opposite (trans, 180°) — only 2.

questions.q: In an octahedral complex, the crystal field splitting energy $\Delta_o$ depends on which factors?
options: colour of the counter ion only
the nature of the ligand, the charge on the metal ion, and whether the metal is 3d, 4d or 5d
molecular formula of the complex only
atomic mass of the metal only
questions.explanation: $\Delta_o$ increases with ligand field strength (spectrochemical series), with increasing metal oxidation state (more charge draws ligands closer), and going down a group (4d, 5d metals split more than 3d).
questions.trick: $\Delta_o$ rises with ligand strength, higher metal charge, and going 3d$\to$4d$\to$5d.

questions.q: Which of the following pairs correctly matches the ligand with its denticity?
questions.explanation: NH$_3$ has a single donor atom (N) and is unidentate; en is bidentate (two N donors), oxalate is bidentate (two O donors), and Cl$^-$ is unidentate.
questions.trick: Denticity: NH$_3$/Cl$^-$ unidentate; en/oxalate bidentate (two donor atoms).

questions.q: The complex $[Cr(NH_3)_6][Co(CN)_6]$ and $[Cr(NH_3)_4(CN)_2][Co(NH_3)_2(CN)_4]$ illustrate which type of isomerism?
options: Coordination isomerism (ligand distribution differs between the cationic and anionic complex)
questions.explanation: When both the cation and anion are complex ions, and the ligands are redistributed differently between the two metal centres while the overall formula stays the same, it is called coordination isomerism.
questions.trick: Ligands swapped between cationic and anionic complex $\to$ coordination isomerism.

questions.q: Which of the following complexes shows sp$^3$ hybridisation and is paramagnetic?
questions.explanation: In $[NiCl_4]^{2-}$, weak field Cl$^-$ does not pair the two unpaired $d^8$ electrons, giving sp$^3$ hybridisation, tetrahedral geometry, and paramagnetism; $[Ni(CO)_4]$ has Ni(0), $d^{10}$, diamagnetic sp$^3$.
questions.trick: Weak field Cl$^-$ leaves $d^8$ unpaired $\to$ sp$^3$, tetrahedral, paramagnetic.

questions.q: The number of unpaired electrons in the low-spin octahedral complex $[Fe(CN)_6]^{4-}$ (Fe$^{2+}$, $d^6$) is
questions.explanation: CN$^-$ is a strong field ligand; all six $d^6$ electrons pair up in the lower $t_{2g}$ orbitals ($t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$), leaving zero unpaired electrons (diamagnetic).
questions.trick: Strong field CN$^-$ forces all $d^6$ electrons into $t_{2g}$ $\to$ zero unpaired.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a double salt from a coordination compound?
options: A coordination compound loses its identity in solution, while a double salt retains the identity of its constituent ions
Double salts do not exist in crystalline form
A double salt completely dissociates into simple ions in solution, while a coordination compound retains its complex ion largely intact
questions.explanation: Double salts like Mohr's salt, FeSO$_4$.(NH$_4$)$_2$SO$_4$.6H$_2$O, dissociate completely into their simple constituent ions in solution and lose identity, whereas complex ions like $[Fe(CN)_6]^{4-}$ remain intact and do not give free Fe$^{2+}$ or CN$^-$ tests.
questions.trick: Double salt fully dissociates (loses identity); complex ion stays intact in solution.

questions.q: The IUPAC name of $K_4[Fe(CN)_6]$ is
questions.explanation: The complex anion is named first with ligands alphabetically, then the metal with suffix '-ate' since the ion is anionic, and its oxidation state: Fe is $+2$ since 6 CN$^-$ give $-6$ and overall charge is $-4$, so K$_4$[Fe(CN)$_6$] = potassium hexacyanidoferrate(II).
questions.trick: Balance charge for oxidation state; anionic complex $\to$ metal name ends '-ate'.

questions.q: Which of the following ligands, upon coordination, is classified as a $\pi$-acid (strong field) ligand due to back bonding?
questions.explanation: CO accepts electron density from filled metal d orbitals into its empty $\pi^*$ orbitals (synergic back bonding), which strengthens the metal-ligand bond and makes CO one of the strongest field ligands.
questions.trick: $\pi$-acid ligands (CO) back-bond into empty $\pi^*$ orbitals, becoming strong field.

questions.q: A student is given four complexes and told exactly one shows optical isomerism. Which one is it?
questions.explanation: The cis isomer of $[Co(en)_2Cl_2]^+$ lacks an internal plane of symmetry and is chiral, showing optical isomerism; the trans isomer has a mirror plane and is optically inactive, and the other two are achiral/too symmetric.
questions.trick: Only the isomer lacking an internal mirror plane (cis, unsymmetrical) is optically active.

questions.q: In naming coordination compounds, if the complex ion is a cation and the central metal is iron, the name used is
questions.explanation: When the coordination entity is a cation (or neutral), the metal's usual English name is used (e.g. iron, cobalt); the Latin-derived '-ate' form (ferrate) is used only when the complex ion is an anion.
questions.trick: Cation/neutral complex keeps normal metal name; only anionic complex uses '-ate'.
